title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF ABDON AND HIS 70 SONS RIDING 70 DONKEYS
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD STORY OF ABDON AND HIS 70 SONS RIDING 70 DONKEYS
The Verse Most People Read Too Fast
Hidden among the dramatic battles of Judges, between famous names like Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson, there is a man whose entire story seems to fit into a single verse.
Most readers pass him without stopping.
No giant was slain.
No army was defeated.
No miracle was recorded.
No sermon was preached.
Yet God deliberately preserved one astonishing detail for thousands of years:

"After him, Abdon son of Hillel, from Pirathon, led Israel. He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. He led Israel eight years."
(Judges 12:13–14)
That is all.
At first glance, it sounds like an insignificant family note buried inside Israel's history.
But Scripture never wastes words.
The God who inspired Genesis, Isaiah, Matthew, and Revelation also inspired this sentence.
Why?
Why would the Holy Spirit preserve the fact that Abdon had seventy descendants riding seventy donkeys?
Why not tell us his greatest accomplishment?
Why not record his victories?
Why mention the donkeys?
The answer reveals a forgotten lesson about leadership, legacy, peace, influence, and a danger that still threatens believers today.
A Nation Emerging From Chaos
To understand Abdon, we must understand the period in which he lived.
The Book of Judges records one of the darkest eras in Israel's history.
Again and again, Israel abandoned God.
Again and again, God allowed oppression.
Again and again, the people cried out.
Again and again, God raised a deliverer.
The cycle repeated for centuries.
The book eventually summarizes the spiritual condition of the nation with a haunting statement:

"In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes."
(Judges 21:25)
The Hebrew phrase is:

"אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו"
(Ish ha-yashar b'einav)
Literally:
"Each man did what was straight in his own eyes."
Human opinion replaced divine authority.
Personal preference replaced obedience.
Truth became subjective.
The result was social chaos, violence, corruption, and spiritual collapse.
Yet into that darkness stepped Abdon.
A Name That Means Servant
The name Abdon comes from the Hebrew:

עַבְדּוֹן
('Avdon)
Its root is connected to the word:

עֶבֶד
('eved)
Meaning:
"servant."
That alone is remarkable.
A leader remembered for influence and prosperity carried a name associated with service.
This anticipates a truth Jesus would later declare:

"Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant."
(Mark 10:43)
In Greek, Jesus uses the word:

διάκονος
(diakonos)
A servant.
A minister.
One who attends to others.
The kingdom of God consistently reverses worldly assumptions.
The greatest are not those who dominate.
The greatest are those who serve.
Abdon's name quietly points toward that reality.
The Mystery of the Seventy
The detail that captures everyone's attention is the number seventy.
Forty sons.
Thirty grandsons.
Seventy descendants.
Seventy donkeys.
The number seventy carries enormous significance throughout Scripture.
Seventy nations descended from Noah's family in Genesis 10.
Seventy elders assisted Moses in Numbers 11.
Seventy members of Jacob's household entered Egypt.
Jesus later sent out seventy disciples to proclaim the Kingdom of God.
In biblical thought, seventy often symbolizes fullness, completeness, and widespread influence.
The text does not explicitly state symbolism here.
However, the number would certainly have caught the attention of ancient readers.
Abdon's family represented remarkable growth, stability, and influence.
This was not merely a household.
This was a dynasty.
The Donkeys Were Not an Accident
Modern readers often miss the significance of the donkeys.
In our culture, mentioning a donkey sounds almost humorous.
In ancient Israel, it communicated something very different.
Donkeys were symbols of status, authority, wealth, and peaceful leadership.
Kings rode donkeys.
Princes rode donkeys.
Judges rode donkeys.
Military commanders often rode horses.
Civil rulers often rode donkeys.
When Solomon was publicly recognized as David's successor, he rode the king's mule.
The image communicated legitimate authority.
Thus, seventy descendants riding seventy donkeys was a public declaration.
Abdon's household possessed influence throughout the land.
This family was respected.
Recognized.
Established.
Prosperous.
Secure.
For a nation emerging from instability, this was remarkable.
The Peace Hidden Between the Lines
One fascinating aspect of Abdon's story is what Scripture does not say.
It records no battles.
No invasions.
No military crises.
No national disasters.
No civil wars.
The silence itself may be significant.
Abdon appears during a relatively peaceful period.
Sometimes God's greatest blessing is not dramatic victory.
Sometimes it is stability.
Sometimes the miracle is not surviving a storm.
Sometimes the miracle is having no storm at all.
Many believers overlook this truth.
We celebrate dramatic testimonies.
We applaud extraordinary rescues.
We share stories of impossible breakthroughs.
Yet quiet faithfulness is often just as miraculous.
A stable marriage.
Children walking with God.
Years of integrity.
A peaceful home.
Steady obedience.
These rarely become headlines.
Yet heaven notices them.
Abdon's story reminds us that not every divine blessing arrives wrapped in drama.
The Hidden Warning
Yet there is another side to this story.
Many scholars have noted that the emphasis on Abdon's large family resembles references to other judges whose influence became concentrated within their own households.
The text does not condemn Abdon.
Scripture never explicitly criticizes him.
However, the repeated mention of large ruling families throughout Judges can create an important tension.
Was leadership becoming hereditary?
Were powerful families beginning to resemble royal dynasties?
The Book of Judges repeatedly shows Israel drifting toward human systems that would eventually culminate in demands for a king.
The warning remains relevant.
Blessings can become idols.
Success can become self-sufficiency.
Influence can become pride.
A godly legacy is beautiful.
But family influence must never replace dependence upon God.
Every generation must choose faith for itself.
Seventy descendants could not guarantee seventy faithful hearts.
Only God can transform hearts.
The Greater Servant-King
Ultimately, Abdon's story points beyond itself.
His descendants rode donkeys as symbols of authority.
Centuries later, another ruler entered Jerusalem riding a donkey.
Not seventy donkeys.
One donkey.
Not surrounded by powerful sons.
Surrounded by ordinary disciples.
Not establishing earthly prestige.
Moving toward a Roman cross.
Matthew records the event as the fulfillment of prophecy.
The crowds expected military triumph.
Instead, they received a suffering King.
The Hebrew prophet Zechariah had written:

"Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey."
(Zechariah 9:9)
The Greek New Testament records Jesus entering Jerusalem in humility.
The King above all kings deliberately chose the animal associated with peaceful rule.
Not because He lacked power.
Because He possessed perfect power.
The donkey that symbolized authority in Abdon's day became a prophetic sign pointing toward Christ.
The servant-leader named Abdon foreshadowed the ultimate Servant-King.
The Legacy Question
Abdon led Israel for only eight years.
Most believers know almost nothing about him.
Yet thousands of years later we still discuss his life because God preserved a few inspired lines.
That raises a sobering question.
What kind of legacy are we building?
Not what kind of image.
Not what kind of platform.
Not what kind of reputation.
Legacy.
Abdon had seventy descendants riding seventy donkeys.
Many today have social media audiences, professional achievements, business success, educational accomplishments, and public recognition.
But when heaven records our story, what will matter?
Will it be wealth?
Influence?
Position?
Or faithfulness?
One day every earthly symbol of status will disappear.
The donkeys will be gone.
The titles will fade.
The applause will end.
The only kingdom that remains forever belongs to Jesus Christ.
The ancient Aramaic-speaking believers would later proclaim:

"מָרַנָא תָא"
(Marana Tha)
"Our Lord, come."
And that remains the cry of every faithful disciple.
Because the goal was never merely to leave behind successful children, prosperous households, or respected names.
The goal is to leave behind evidence that we belonged to Christ.
Perhaps that is why God preserved Abdon's story.
Not because of the seventy.
Not because of the donkeys.
Not because of the influence.
But because every earthly legacy eventually points us toward the One whose kingdom will never end.
And when the final chapter of history is written, no one will be asking who rode the donkeys.
They will be asking who followed the King.
One day every earthly throne will be empty, but the Lamb will still be reigning.
